content: Errors arising from assay failure, environmental conditions, or operator performance must be identified and corrected before test results are reported. Quality control (QC) is a multi-step process with specific checkpoints throughout the testing process. Pre-analytical phase (before testing): The temperature of the testing area must be checked daily to ensure it is within the manufacturer’s recommended range. Testing should not proceed if the room temperature is outside the acceptable range. Daily checks must confirm that sufficient stocks of test kits and required consumables are available. Analytical phase (during testing): QC specimens, such as test kit controls or external/third-party QC specimens, must be run, and their results must fall within pre-established QC acceptance limits. Post-analytical phase (after testing): The HIV status report to be provided to the client must be double-checked for accuracy. Data entry into the testing register must also be double-checked to ensure accuracy. Internal QC refers to processes within the assay that verify whether the procedure is functioning correctly. For rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), the appearance of a control line or spot is an example of internal QC. However, most RDTs only control for liquid flow along the test strip and do not verify specimen addition. Test kit controls (positive and negative controls) may be supplied by the assay manufacturer and are standard for most in vitro diagnostic (IVD) formats, except for RDTs. Few HIV RDTs include accompanying test kit controls. External third-party QC materials should be used in addition to internal QC or test kit controls. These materials are prepared and validated by a QC provider, preferably an experienced commercial entity or an institution designated by national authorities, such as a national reference laboratory. These materials can be manufactured in bulk and stored for extended periods, reducing costs associated with acquisition, characterization, and validation. Each batch of in-house QC material must be tested for homogeneity and stability. External QC specimens for process control should be run: Weekly, preferably at the beginning of the week. For any new operator, including trained staff who have not conducted testing recently. For each new lot or shipment of test kits. When environmental conditions (e.g., temperature or humidity) fall outside the manufacturer’s recommended range. If external QC results deviate from expected outcomes, all test results since the last valid QC run are considered “out-of-control.” In such cases, retesting all individuals tested during this period should be considered. Implementation guidelines: Establish criteria for specimen acceptance or rejection, storage, retention, disposal, and referral to another site for testing. Define QC criteria for qualitative and quantitative assays with established limits of acceptability. Information management: Information management involves systems (paper or electronic) for recording, storing, and retrieving data, including test results, raw data, and communications with clients. All testing personnel must minimize transcription errors. Ideally, a second reader should perform a blinded interpretation of visually read assays. If the two readers agree, the result can be accepted. Disagreements should be resolved by a third reader. Documentation and record-keeping: Documents include policies, procedures, and work instructions for all aspects of the testing service and its quality management system (QMS). These documents must be approved before use, reviewed annually, revised as needed, and removed when obsolete. Proper documentation ensures that HIV status reports are delivered to the correct individual. Records generated from testing activities must be completed accurately and securely stored for up to five years. Occurrence management: Occurrence management involves detecting and documenting non-conformances and implementing necessary corrections. Non-conformances may include a lack of documented procedures or failure to follow them. Data sources for identifying non-conformances include internal audit reports, supervisory visit reports, QC data, and external quality assessment (EQA) results. Assessment: Testing services should conduct both internal and external assessments to ensure quality. Internal audits, performed by supervisors or district health teams, should observe testing practices at least annually, preferably every three to six months. EQA schemes, such as proficiency testing, are critical for ensuring the accuracy and reliability of test results. Providers of proficiency panels should be ISO-accredited or actively pursuing accreditation. Retesting: All individuals newly diagnosed as HIV-positive should be retested before initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) to identify diagnostic errors before starting lifelong treatment. Process improvement: Testing services must identify areas for improvement, plan and implement changes, and evaluate their impact. Corrective actions address the root cause of a problem, while preventive actions reduce the likelihood of recurrence. Data from QC, EQA, and process control activities can guide these actions. Client service: Programs must ensure client satisfaction by meeting expectations for quality and delivering accurate results promptly. Feedback from clients can be gathered through exit interviews or suggestion boxes. Privacy and confidentiality must be maintained at all times. Facilities and safety: Testing sites must be clean, comfortable, and well-lit, with adequate ventilation and proper waste disposal systems. Universal precautions must be followed to prevent harm to clients and staff. Facilities should also be organized to protect client confidentiality, such as providing separate waiting areas for those requiring additional testing. For HIV testing conducted outside of facilities, programs must ensure that providers can perform testing safely for both themselves and their clients.
